claim: KPNB1 is an importin β component of the ncRNA repressor of nuclear factor of activated T cells (NRON) ribonucleoprotein complex.
source: Here, we report that KPNB1, an importin β component of the ncRNA repressor of nuclear factor of activated T cells (NRON) ribonucleoprotein complex, mediates nuclear translocation and repressor function of the PER/CRY complex.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations to previous work on NRON complex composition.

claim: KPNB1 mediates nuclear translocation and repressor function of the PER/CRY complex.
source: Here, we report that KPNB1, an importin β component of the ncRNA repressor of nuclear factor of activated T cells (NRON) ribonucleoprotein complex, mediates nuclear translocation and repressor function of the PER/CRY complex.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental approaches including RNAi, microscopy, and functional assays.

claim: RNAi depletion of KPNB1 traps the PER/CRY complex in the cytoplasm by blocking nuclear entry of PER proteins in human cells.
source: RNAi depletion of KPNB1 traps the PER/CRY complex in the cytoplasm by blocking nuclear entry of PER proteins in human cells.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and immunoblot data shown in Figure 1.

claim: KPNB1 interacts mainly with PER proteins.
source: KPNB1 interacts mainly with PER proteins and directs PER/CRY nuclear transport in a circadian fashion.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: KPNB1 directs PER/CRY nuclear transport in a circadian fashion.
source: KPNB1 interacts mainly with PER proteins and directs PER/CRY nuclear transport in a circadian fashion.
evidence: This is supported by time-course experiments in mouse liver showing rhythmic nuclear accumulation of KPNB1 with PER/CRY proteins (Figure 2D).

claim: KPNB1 regulates the PER/CRY nuclear entry and repressor function independently of importin α.
source: Interestingly, KPNB1 regulates the PER/CRY nuclear entry and repressor function, independently of importin α, its classical partner.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with KPNB1 mutants lacking importin α binding domain (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and knockdown experiments of importin α isoforms (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, 3).

claim: Inducible inhibition of the conserved Drosophila importin β in lateral neurons abolishes behavioral rhythms in flies.
source: Moreover, inducible inhibition of the conserved Drosophila importin β in lateral neurons abolishes behavioral rhythms in flies.
evidence: This is supported by locomotor activity monitoring of flies with ketel RNAi expression (Figure 5).

claim: KPNB1 is required for timely nuclear import of PER/CRY in the negative feedback regulation of the circadian clock.
source: Collectively, these data show that KPNB1 is required for timely nuclear import of PER/CRY in the negative feedback regulation of the circadian clock.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from all experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Nearly all organisms have circadian clocks, internal timing systems that anticipate and adapt physiology and behavior to daily changes in the light–dark cycle.
source: Nearly all organisms have circadian clocks, internal timing systems that anticipate and adapt physiology and behavior to daily changes in the light–dark cycle.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about circadian clocks.

claim: In eukaryotes, the clock is an interlocked transcriptional–translational feedback loop.
source: In eukaryotes, the clock is an interlocked transcriptional–translational feedback loop, which drives rhythmic expression of both core clock genes that make up the oscillator and clock-output genes that drive biological rhythms.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the molecular mechanism of circadian clocks.

claim: Many components and the molecular mechanism of the circadian clock are conserved between flies and mammals.
source: Many components and the molecular mechanism of the circadian clock are conserved between flies and mammals.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about evolutionary conservation of clock mechanisms.

claim: Conserved components include the bHLH-PAS transactivators, CLOCK/NPAS2 (fly Clk) and BMAL1 (fly Cyc).
source: Conserved components include the bHLH-PAS transactivators, CLOCK/NPAS2 (fly Clk) and BMAL1 (fly Cyc).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about conserved clock components.

claim: The CLOCK/BMAL1 heterodimer binds E-box elements in the promoters of PER1/PER2/PER3 and CRY1/CRY2 genes.
source: This heterodimer binds E-box elements in the promoters of two families of transcriptional repressors, the PER1/PER2/PER3 (fly Per) and CRY1/CRY2 (fly Cry) genes.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about clock gene regulation, supported by citation (Panda et al., 2002).

claim: Once translated, PERs and CRYs accumulate in a cytoplasmic complex and then translocate into the nucleus to repress the CLOCK-BMAL1 heterodimer.
source: Once translated, PERs and CRYs (Per and Tim in flies) accumulate in a cytoplasmic complex and then translocate into the nucleus to repress the CLOCK-BMAL1 heterodimer, thereby repressing their own transcription (Panda et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the negative feedback loop, supported by citation.

claim: KPNB1 is a nuclear import receptor that mediates docking of nuclear localization signal (NLS)-containing cargo bound to importin α to the nuclear envelope.
source: KPNB1 is a nuclear import receptor that mediates docking of nuclear localization signal (NLS)-containing cargo bound to importin α to the nuclear envelope, thereby facilitating nuclear entry of the target protein (van der Watt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about KPNB1 function, supported by citation.

claim: KPNB1 can directly recognize cargo and facilitate nuclear transport independently of importin α.
source: KPNB1 can also directly recognize the cargo and facilitate nuclear transport independently of importin α (Lam et al., 1999; Forwood et al., 2001; Ghildyal et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about alternative KPNB1 function, supported by citations.

claim: PER1/2 and CRY1/2 contain a functional NLS for their nuclear entry and transcriptional feedback function.
source: In several intensive molecular analyses, PER1/2 and CRY1/2, have been found to contain a functional NLS for their nuclear entry and transcriptional feedback function (Vielhaber et al., 2000; Miyazaki et al., 2001; Hirayama et al., 2003; Zhu et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Nucleocytoplasmic shuttling of PER proteins, in conjunction with protein dimerization, phosphorylation and turnover, is critical for clock function.
source: Furthermore, nucleocytoplasmic shuttling of PER proteins, in conjunction with protein dimerization, phosphorylation and turnover, is critical for clock function (Yagita et al., 2000, 2002).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Nuclear transport of mouse Cry2 is mediated by its direct interaction with importin α family members (RCH1, QIP-1, NPI-2).
source: Interestingly, a previous biochemical and cellular study reported that nuclear transport of mouse Cry2 is mediated by its direct interaction with importin α family members (RCH1, QIP-1, NPI-2) (Sakakida et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study, supported by citation.

claim: The functional relevance of importin α family members in the clock was not evaluated in previous studies.
source: However, the functional relevance of these factors in the clock was not evaluated (Sakakida et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of previous research.

claim: KPNB1 was identified as a key nuclear importin component of NRON RNA-protein-scaffold complex containing several kinases, CKIε, GSK3β, and DYRK2.
source: In recent studies, KPNB1 was identified as a key nuclear importin component of ncRNA repressor of nuclear factor of activated T cells (NFAT) (NRON) (lncRNA repressor of the NFAT) RNA-protein-scaffold complex containing several kinases, CKIε, GSK3β, and DYRK2 that regulate NFAT phosphorylation and nuclear translocation in human and Drosophila cells (Gwack et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2011; Sharma et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge from recent studies, supported by citations.

claim: CKIε, GSK3β, and DYRK2 regulate NFAT phosphorylation and nuclear translocation in human and Drosophila cells.
source: In recent studies, KPNB1 was identified as a key nuclear importin component of ncRNA repressor of nuclear factor of activated T cells (NFAT) (NRON) (lncRNA repressor of the NFAT) RNA-protein-scaffold complex containing several kinases, CKIε, GSK3β, and DYRK2 that regulate NFAT phosphorylation and nuclear translocation in human and Drosophila cells (Gwack et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2011; Sharma et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Most kinases in the NRON complex are also well-known to regulate phosphorylation-related proteolysis and nuclear entry of circadian clock proteins.
source: Notably, most of these kinases are also well-known to regulate phosphorylation-related proteolysis and nuclear entry of circadian clock proteins.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the dual roles of these kinases.

claim: KPNB1 knockdown completely blocked nuclear accumulation of PER1 and PER2.
source: Interestingly, in immunofluorescence (IF) analysis of cells expressing several flag-tagged clock proteins, knockdown of KPNB1 completely blocked (PER1, PER2), partly blocked (CRY1), or didn't significantly block (CRY2, REVERBα, CLOCK, CHRONO [Anafi et al., 2014]) nuclear accumulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: KPNB1 knockdown partly blocked nuclear accumulation of CRY1.
source: Interestingly, in immunofluorescence (IF) analysis of cells expressing several flag-tagged clock proteins, knockdown of KPNB1 completely blocked (PER1, PER2), partly blocked (CRY1), or didn't significantly block (CRY2, REVERBα, CLOCK, CHRONO [Anafi et al., 2014]) nuclear accumulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: KPNB1 knockdown didn't significantly block nuclear accumulation of CRY2, REVERBα, CLOCK, and CHRONO.
source: Interestingly, in immunofluorescence (IF) analysis of cells expressing several flag-tagged clock proteins, knockdown of KPNB1 completely blocked (PER1, PER2), partly blocked (CRY1), or didn't significantly block (CRY2, REVERBα, CLOCK, CHRONO [Anafi et al., 2014]) nuclear accumulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: KPNB1 knockdown markedly blocked PER1 and PER2 localization in cells expressing Venus-tagged proteins.
source: Similar to the flag-tagged proteins, microscopy and immunoblot analysis of cells expressing the Venus (V)-tagged clock proteins (PER1-V, PER2-V, CRY1-V, CRY2-V), KPNB1 knockdown markedly blocked PER1 and PER2 localization and slightly or negligibly effected CRY1 and CRY2 nuclear localization (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy and immunoblot data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: KPNB1 knockdown slightly or negligibly affected CRY1 and CRY2 nuclear localization in cells expressing Venus-tagged proteins.
source: Similar to the flag-tagged proteins, microscopy and immunoblot analysis of cells expressing the Venus (V)-tagged clock proteins (PER1-V, PER2-V, CRY1-V, CRY2-V), KPNB1 knockdown markedly blocked PER1 and PER2 localization and slightly or negligibly effected CRY1 and CRY2 nuclear localization (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy and immunoblot data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: PER and CRY proteins work together.
source: In many previous studies, PER and CRY proteins have been shown to work together (Tamanini et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: KPNB1 depletion significantly impaired nuclear localization of various combinations of PER and CRY proteins.
source: The BiFC assay showed that KPNB1 depletion significantly impaired nuclear localization of various combinations of PER and CRY proteins (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by BiFC assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Nuclear accumulation of the PER2/CRY1 complex was totally blocked by KPNB1 knockdown.
source: Notably, nuclear accumulation of the PER2/CRY1 complex was totally blocked by KPNB1 knockdown (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by BiFC assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: KPNB1 depletion substantially increased cytoplasmic accumulation of endogenous PER1/2 and CRY1/2 proteins.
source: In addition to ectopically expressed clock proteins, KPNB1 depletion substantially increased cytoplasmic accumulation of endogenous PER1/2 and CRY1/2 proteins thus reducing their relative levels in nuclei in most cells (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: KPNB1 serves as an integral nuclear transport receptor of the PER/CRY complex.
source: Taken together, these evidence show that KPNB1 serves as an integral nuclear transport receptor of the PER/CRY complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 1 and related supplements.

claim: KPNB1 interacted more strongly with PER1 and PER2 proteins than either CRY1 or CRY2.
source: KPNB1 interacted more strongly with PER1 and PER2 proteins than either CRY1 or CRY2 (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: PER proteins may play the leading role in PERs/CRYs nuclear translocation with KPNB1.
source: This suggested that PER proteins may play the leading role in PERs/CRYs nuclear translocation with KPNB1.
evidence: This is inferred from the stronger interaction of KPNB1 with PER proteins compared to CRY proteins.

claim: KPNB1 co-localized with both cytoplasmic and nuclear PER2.
source: In support of this, by IF KPNB1 co-localized with both cytoplasmic and nuclear PER2 (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: KPNB1 strongly interacted with the endogenous PER2 in mouse liver tissue extracts.
source: Correspondingly, KPNB1 strongly interacted with the endogenous PER2 in co-immunoprecipitation analysis using mouse liver tissue extracts (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: KPNB1 exhibited a circadian pattern of nucleocytoplasmic localization with its nuclear abundance peaking at circadian time (CT) 14–18.
source: By immunoblot analysis, KPNB1 exhibited a circadian pattern of nucleocytoplasmic localization with its nuclear abundance peaking at circadian time (CT) 14–18, when the intensive nuclear accumulation of PER2 and CRY1 occurred (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot analysis of mouse liver tissue extracts shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Intensive nuclear accumulation of PER2 and CRY1 occurred at circadian time (CT) 14–18.
source: By immunoblot analysis, KPNB1 exhibited a circadian pattern of nucleocytoplasmic localization with its nuclear abundance peaking at circadian time (CT) 14–18, when the intensive nuclear accumulation of PER2 and CRY1 occurred (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot analysis of mouse liver tissue extracts shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Significant decrease of mRNA expression of E-box dependent clock genes (Per1, Dbp, Nr1d1, Nr1d2) occurred in the nuclear accumulation phase of PER/CRY.
source: Concomitantly, we observed the significant decrease of mRNA expression of E-box dependent clock genes (Per1, Dbp, Nr1d1, Nr1d2) targeted by the clock repressors in their nuclear accumulation phase (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: KPNB1 is responsible for circadian nuclear import and repressor activity of the PER/CRY complex in clock gene expression in mouse liver.
source: Thus, these data clearly suggest that KPNB1 is responsible for circadian nuclear import and repressor activity of the PER/CRY complex in clock gene expression in mouse liver.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the circadian expression data in mouse liver.

claim: KPNB1 knockdown substantially elevated Per1 promoter activity.
source: To investigate the role of KPNB1 in clock function, we used RNAi to knockdown KPNB1 in U2 OS cells and found substantially elevated Per1 promoter activity, consistent with the hypothesis that this knockdown inhibited the localization and function of the PER/CRY complex (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Depletion of TNPO1 and CSE1L did not significantly affect PER/CRY repressor activities.
source: In contrast, the parallel depletion of the other NRON complex nucleocytoplasmic transport proteins, TNPO1, CSE1L, did not significantly affect their repressor activities (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, [Willingham et al., 2005]).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: ChIP analysis revealed significantly less recruitment of both PER1 and PER2 to the CLOCK/BMAL1 responsive element in KPNB1-depleted U2 OS cells.
source: In support of this, chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) analysis targeting the first E-box region of human PER1 (hPer1) promoter revealed significantly less recruitment of both PER1 and PER2 to the CLOCK/BMAL1 responsive element in the KPNB1-depleted U2 OS cells (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 3B–D.

claim: The overall expression levels of several E-box dependent genes (PER1, CRY1, DBP, REV-ERBβ) were upregulated as a result of KPNB1 knockdown.
source: Moreover, the overall expression levels of several E-box dependent genes (PER1, CRY1, DBP, REV-ERBβ) were upregulated as a result of KPNB1 knockdown (Figure 3E), consistent with loss of repressor function.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Overexpression of KPNB1 markedly down-regulated CLOCK/BMAL1-activated PER1 transcription.
source: Conversely, overexpression of KPNB1 markedly down-regulated CLOCK/BMAL1-activated PER1 transcription, probably by facilitating PER/CRY localization to the nucleus (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: KPNB1 overexpression significantly down-regulated endogenous mRNA expression of E-box-regulated genes with no significant effect on BMAL1 expression.
source: Correspondingly, KPNB1 overexpression significantly down-regulated endogenous mRNA expression of these E-box-regulated genes with no significant effect on BMAL1 expression (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Deletion of the importin α binding domain of KPNB1 did not significantly affect the transcriptional regulation.
source: Notably, the KPNB1 activity was not dependent on importin α, a well-known nuclear transport partner, as deletion of the importin α binding domain of KPNB1 did not significantly affect the transcriptional regulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C) (Kutay et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: Knockdown of KPNB1 in U2 OS cells severely disturbed circadian bioluminescence reporter activity driven by the Per2 promoter.
source: Importantly, knockdown of KPNB1 in U2 OS cells severely disturbed circadian bioluminescence reporter activity driven by the Per2 promoter, whereas depletion of importin α1 (KPNA2) or importin α5 (KPNA1) did not affect the circadian rhythmicity (Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by bioluminescence recording data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Depletion of importin α1 (KPNA2) or importin α5 (KPNA1) did not affect the circadian rhythmicity.
source: Importantly, knockdown of KPNB1 in U2 OS cells severely disturbed circadian bioluminescence reporter activity driven by the Per2 promoter, whereas depletion of importin α1 (KPNA2) or importin α5 (KPNA1) did not affect the circadian rhythmicity (Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by bioluminescence recording data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: Most of the other importin α isoforms were not critical for circadian rhythmicity.
source: These knockdown phenotypes correspond to previous reports showing that most of the other importin α isoforms were not critical for circadian rhythmicity (Wu et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge from previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: KPNA2 or KPNA1 depletion did not alter PER2 nuclear localization.
source: In conjunction with these results, fluorescence microscopy analysis revealed that KPNA2 or KPNA1 depletion did not alter PER2 nuclear localization, which was completely blocked by KPNB1 depletion in U2 OS cells stably expressing PER2-Venus (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D, Figure 4—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 3C,D.

claim: KPNB1 depletion severely disrupted circadian transcription of several clock genes (PER1, PER2) in dexamethasone (Dex)-synchronized cells.
source: On the other hand, KPNB1 depletion severely disrupted circadian transcription of several clock genes (PER1, PER2) in dexamethasone (Dex)-synchronized cells with altered nuclear accumulation of PER and CRY proteins (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative RT-PCR and immunoblot data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: KPNB1 depletion altered nuclear accumulation of PER and CRY proteins in Dex-synchronized cells.
source: On the other hand, KPNB1 depletion severely disrupted circadian transcription of several clock genes (PER1, PER2) in dexamethasone (Dex)-synchronized cells with altered nuclear accumulation of PER and CRY proteins (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: KPNB1 gates PER and CRY localization to the nucleus independently of importin α.
source: Taken together, these data show that KPNB1 gates PER and CRY localization to the nucleus independently of importin α and plays an indispensable role in negative feedback regulation of the circadian clock in human cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: KPNB1 plays an indispensable role in negative feedback regulation of the circadian clock in human cells.
source: Taken together, these data show that KPNB1 gates PER and CRY localization to the nucleus independently of importin α and plays an indispensable role in negative feedback regulation of the circadian clock in human cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: 62% of flies expressing UAS ketel RNAi in central clock cells exhibited no rhythms in constant darkness.
source: Behavioral analysis of flies expressing UAS ketel RNAi in central clock cells, targeted by the relatively weak Pigment dispersing factor (Pdf)-Gal4 driver, revealed that 62% of flies exhibited no rhythms in constant darkness (DD).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral analysis data shown in Figure 5 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: 38% of flies expressing UAS ketel RNAi in central clock cells were rhythmic, but their rhythm strength determined by fast Fourier transform (FFT) value was low.
source: Although 38% of flies were rhythmic, their rhythm strength determined by fast Fourier transform (FFT) value was low (Figure 5A–C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral analysis data shown in Figure 5A–C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: With a strong tim-UAS-Gal4 driver that is expressed in all clock cells, 100% of flies were arrhythmic.
source: With a strong tim-UAS-Gal4 driver that is expressed in all clock cells, 100% of flies were arrhythmic (Figure 5A,B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral analysis data shown in Figure 5A,B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Conditional knockdown of ketel in adult PDF+ neurons resulted in weak to arrhythmic locomotor activity.
source: After 6–7 days in constant darkness, this conditional knockdown of ketel also resulted in weak to arrhythmic locomotor activity (Figure 5D, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral analysis data shown in Figure 5D and Supplementary file 1.

claim: 81% of flies with conditional knockdown of ketel were arrhythmic and the rest showed weak rhythmicity with low FFT values.
source: 81% of flies were arrhythmic and the rest showed weak rhythmicity with low FFT values (Figure 5E, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral analysis data shown in Figure 5E and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Importin β in PDF+ neurons is required for normal locomotor rhythms in adult flies.
source: These results show that importin β in PDF+ neurons is required for normal locomotor rhythms in adult flies.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral analysis data in flies.

claim: In ketel knockdown flies, PER levels were low and primarily cytoplasmic in large LNvs at ZT1.
source: In ketel knockdown flies, PER levels were low and primarily cytoplasmic in large LNvs, while PER staining was intensely nuclear in control flies (Figure 5F,G).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5F,G.

claim: PER staining was intensely nuclear in control flies at ZT1.
source: In ketel knockdown flies, PER levels were low and primarily cytoplasmic in large LNvs, while PER staining was intensely nuclear in control flies (Figure 5F,G).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5F,G.

claim: The small LNvs were undetectable in ketel RNAi transgenic flies.
source: The small LNvs were undetectable in ketel RNAi transgenic flies, as is also the case in other arrhythmic fly mutants such as Clk and cyc (Figure 5F, right panel images) (Park et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5F and comparison to previous studies.

claim: Ketel mediates the nuclear localization of PER in Drosophila.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that like mammalian importin β, Ketel mediates the nuclear localization of PER, and consequently, is required for functioning of the core circadian clock.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fly behavioral and immunofluorescence data.

claim: Ketel is required for functioning of the core circadian clock in Drosophila.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that like mammalian importin β, Ketel mediates the nuclear localization of PER, and consequently, is required for functioning of the core circadian clock.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fly behavioral and immunofluorescence data.

claim: Timely nuclear translocation of the PER/CRY (or Per/Tim) repressor complex is a critical and conserved step in maintaining rhythmicity in metazoans.
source: Timely nuclear translocation of the PER/CRY (or Per/Tim) repressor complex is a critical and conserved step in maintaining rhythmicity in metazoans.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about circadian clock mechanisms.

claim: The functional carrier molecules responsible for nuclear localization of the feedback regulators have yet to be determined.
source: However, the functional carrier molecules responsible for nuclear localization of the feedback regulators have yet to be determined.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in scientific knowledge that this study addresses.

claim: This study provides the first evidence that KPNB1 plays a key role as a nuclear transporter of the PER/CRY complex in negative feedback repression in both mammalian and fly clocks.
source: Our study provides the first evidence that KPNB1 plays a key role as a nuclear transporter of the PER/CRY complex in negative feedback repression in both mammalian and fly clocks (Figure 6).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all experimental data.

claim: Phosphorylation and nuclear translocation of PERs and CRYs are closely coupled.
source: Many mammalian and Drosophila clock studies have shown that phosphorylation and nuclear translocation of PERs and CRYs are closely coupled (Gallego and Virshup, 2007).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: CKIε, GSK3β, and DYRK2 are clock kinases in both mammals and flies.
source: We noted that CKIε, GSK3β, and DYRK2, clock kinases in both mammals and flies, are also constituents of the NRON complex, which regulates cytoplasmic to nuclear translocation of NFAT and consequently its function in the immune systems (Willingham et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The NRON complex regulates cytoplasmic to nuclear translocation of NFAT and consequently its function in the immune systems.
source: We noted that CKIε, GSK3β, and DYRK2, clock kinases in both mammals and flies, are also constituents of the NRON complex, which regulates cytoplasmic to nuclear translocation of NFAT and consequently its function in the immune systems (Willingham et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: KPNB1 is the major transport receptor for NFAT nuclear entry and activity upon its dephosphorylation.
source: Subsequent study showed that KPNB1 is the major transport receptor for NFAT nuclear entry and activity upon its dephosphorylation (Sharma et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: KPNB1 knockdown trapped PER and CRY proteins at the nuclear membrane, preventing their nuclear accumulation.
source: Thus, we investigated the role of KPNB1 on nuclear localization of PER/CRY complex (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1). We found that KPNB1 knockdown trapped PER and CRY proteins at the nuclear membrane, preventing their nuclear accumulation.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: KPNB1 knockdown significantly relieved PER1 transcriptional repression by the PER/CRY complex.
source: Consistent with this, in our transcriptional study, we found KPNB1 knockdown significantly relieved PER1 transcriptional repression by the PER/CRY complex.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3.

claim: TNPO1 and CSE1L did not interact with PER or CRY proteins.
source: Depletion of the other NRON complex translocation factors, TNPO1 and CSE1L, did not (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), nor did they interact with PER or CRY proteins (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as unpublished data from the study.

claim: KPNB1 has a specific role as a nuclear transport receptor directly involved in negative feedback regulation of the core clock, in addition to its previously described role in NFAT signaling.
source: These data suggest a specific role of KPNB1 as a nuclear transport receptor directly involved in negative feedback regulation of the core clock, in addition to its previously described role in NFAT signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Both TNPO1 and CSE1L displayed circadian gene expression in various mouse tissues.
source: Despite not playing a role in PER/CRY function, both TNPO1 and CSE1L displayed circadian gene expression in various mouse tissues, and also affected circadian period length (TNPO1) or were required for cellular rhythms (CSE1L) when silenced ([Pizarro et al., 2013], data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by citation and unpublished data.

claim: TNPO1 affected circadian period length when silenced.
source: Despite not playing a role in PER/CRY function, both TNPO1 and CSE1L displayed circadian gene expression in various mouse tissues, and also affected circadian period length (TNPO1) or were required for cellular rhythms (CSE1L) when silenced ([Pizarro et al., 2013], data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by citation and unpublished data.

claim: CSE1L was required for cellular rhythms when silenced.
source: Despite not playing a role in PER/CRY function, both TNPO1 and CSE1L displayed circadian gene expression in various mouse tissues, and also affected circadian period length (TNPO1) or were required for cellular rhythms (CSE1L) when silenced ([Pizarro et al., 2013], data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by citation and unpublished data.

claim: TNPO1 exhibits circadian expression profiles in its mRNA in SCN.
source: Interestingly, the recent in situ hybridization analysis showed that TNPO1 exhibits circadian expression profiles in its mRNA in SCN (Sato et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: TNPO1 and CSE1L may play a role in mammalian clock function independent from PER/CRY, perhaps regulating import and export of other clock related components.
source: Thus, these proteins may also play a role in mammalian clock function independent from PER/CRY, perhaps regulating import and export of other clock related components.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed effects of TNPO1 and CSE1L on circadian rhythms.

claim: KPNB1 strongly interacted with PER proteins.
source: Notably, in our biochemical analyses, KPNB1 strongly interacted with PER proteins and exhibited rhythmic nucleocytoplasmic localization and concurrent nuclear accumulation with PER/CRY in transcriptional repression phase (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2.

claim: KPNB1 exhibited rhythmic nucleocytoplasmic localization and concurrent nuclear accumulation with PER/CRY in transcriptional repression phase.
source: Notably, in our biochemical analyses, KPNB1 strongly interacted with PER proteins and exhibited rhythmic nucleocytoplasmic localization and concurrent nuclear accumulation with PER/CRY in transcriptional repression phase (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: KPNB1 drives circadian nuclear entry of PER/CRY.
source: These data suggest KPNB1 drives circadian nuclear entry of PER/CRY.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the biochemical data.

claim: Intracellular calcium levels regulate importin β-dependent nuclear import.
source: Most recently, it was reported that intracellular calcium levels regulate importin β-dependent nuclear import (Kaur et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: KPNB1 nuclear-translocates NFAT immediately after stimulation dependent intracellular calcium influx.
source: Further, a previous model suggests that KPNB1 nuclear-translocates NFAT immediately after stimulation dependent intracellular calcium influx (Sharma et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Periodic Ca2+ influx in the cytosol is a critical process for circadian pacemaker function.
source: In this regard, several studies have demonstrated the important function of Ca2+ dynamics in circadian clock regulation. For example, periodic Ca2+ influx in the cytosol, resulting from circadian variation in membrane potential or by the release of Ca(2+) from ryanodine-sensitive stores in SCN neurons, is a critical process for circadian pacemaker function (Ikeda et al., 2003; Lundkvist et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cytosolic Ca2+ rhythms contribute to driving timely nuclear localization of KPNB1 and its PER/CRY cargo as a critical step in negative feedback regulation of the clock.
source: Based on this evidence, we postulate that cytosolic Ca2+ rhythms contribute to driving timely nuclear localization of KPNB1 and its PER/CRY cargo as a critical step in negative feedback regulation of the clock.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the known roles of calcium in both KPNB1 function and circadian regulation.

claim: In early models, KPNB1 mediates docking of the importin α/substrate complex in the nuclear pore.
source: In early models, KPNB1 mediates docking of the importin α/substrate complex in the nuclear pore.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about KPNB1 function.

claim: KPNB1 can function as nuclear transport receptor independently of importin α by directly recognizing substrates such as CREB, AP-1 transcription factors, and parathyroid hormone-related protein.
source: More recent evidence shows that KPNB1 can function as nuclear transport receptor independently of importin α by directly recognizing substrates such as CREB, AP-1 transcription factors, and parathyroid hormone-related protein (Lam et al., 1999; Forwood et al., 2001; Ghildyal et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Importin α isoforms (RCH, QIP-1, NPI-2) mediate nuclear localization of CRY2 through direct interactions.
source: Interestingly, a previous report showed that importin α isoforms (RCH, QIP-1, NPI-2) mediate nuclear localization of CRY2 through direct interactions but did not investigate the functional consequence of this interaction (Sakakida et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In mammals KPNB1 mediates nuclear localization of the PER/CRY complex independently of importin α.
source: In this regard, our data suggest that in mammals KPNB1 mediates nuclear localization of the PER/CRY complex independently of importin α, as overexpression of a KPNB1 mutant lacking an importin α interaction domain had a similar phenotype (Figure 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both KPNA2 and KPNA1, when depleted in cells, did not affect circadian rhythmicity or subcellular localization of PER2 or CRY2 protein.
source: Consistent with this, both KPNA2 and KPNA1, the well-known KPNB1 interacting importin alpha proteins (importin α1, importin α5), when depleted in cells, did not affect circadian rhythmicity or subcellular localization of PER2 or CRY2 protein (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1, 2, and 3.

claim: Cytoplasmic retention of PER proteins was accelerated by KPNA2 overexpression in mouse stem cells.
source: In a recent report, cytoplasmic retention of PER proteins was accelerated by KPNA2 overexpression in mouse stem cells (Umemura et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: KPNA2 overexpression substantially reduced cells expressing PER2-Venus protein.
source: However, intriguingly we found that KPNA2 overexpression substantially reduced cells expressing PER2-Venus protein in our imaging studies (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Both the endogenous and overexpressed KPNA2 protein localized predominantly in the nucleus.
source: Moreover, both the endogenous and overexpressed KPNA2 protein localized predominantly in the nucleus, which was confirmed by nuclear cytoplasmic fraction Western analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: KPNA2 might regulate PER2 protein level through an unknown mechanism in U2 OS cells.
source: This suggests that KPNA2 might regulate PER2 protein level through an unknown mechanism in U2 OS cells.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed effects of KPNA2 overexpression.

claim: Different results regarding KPNA2 effects are likely due to the different cell types and species used.
source: Thus, we speculate that these different results are likely due to the different cell types and species used.
evidence: This is a speculation to explain discrepancies between studies.

claim: Knockdown of KPNB1 had strong effects on PER1 and PER2, modest effects on CRY1, and no effect on CRY2 when examining single tagged proteins.
source: On the other hand, knockdown of KPNB1 had strong (PER1, PER2), modest (CRY1), or no effect (CRY2) on single tagged PER and CRY proteins, while it had strong effects on all combinations of PER/CRY complexes (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A–C.

claim: Knockdown of KPNB1 had strong effects on all combinations of PER/CRY complexes.
source: On the other hand, knockdown of KPNB1 had strong (PER1, PER2), modest (CRY1), or no effect (CRY2) on single tagged PER and CRY proteins, while it had strong effects on all combinations of PER/CRY complexes (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by BiFC data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Knockdown of KPNB1 increased cytoplasmic retention of endogenous PER1, PER2, CRY1, and CRY2 to varying degrees, probably through complex interactions.
source: Similarly, knockdown of KPNB1 increased cytoplasmic retention of endogenous PER1, PER2, CRY1, and CRY2 to varying degrees, probably through complex interactions (Figure 1D, Figure1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The PERs mediate interaction with KPNB1 and gate nuclear translocation of PER/CRY complex.
source: The immunoprecipitation analysis showed that KPNB1 interacted strongly with PERs compared with CRYs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A). These data suggest that the PERs mediate interaction with KPNB1 and gate nuclear translocation of PER/CRY complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The nuclear entry of CRY is mainly dependent on PER, in vivo.
source: This is reminiscent of a previous report indicating that the nuclear entry of CRY is mainly dependent on PER, in vivo (Lee et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Knockdown of KPNB1 or its fly ortholog ketel resulted in arrhythmic U2 OS cells or fly locomotor activity rhythms.
source: Finally, knockdown of KPNB1 or its fly ortholog ketel resulted in arrhythmic U2 OS cells or fly locomotor activity rhythms, while knockdown of most of KPNA isoforms had no significant effect on the rhythm (Figure 4, Figure 5, Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4, Figure 5, and Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Knockdown of most of KPNA isoforms had no significant effect on the rhythm.
source: Finally, knockdown of KPNB1 or its fly ortholog ketel resulted in arrhythmic U2 OS cells or fly locomotor activity rhythms, while knockdown of most of KPNA isoforms had no significant effect on the rhythm (Figure 4, Figure 5, Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: KPNB1 plays a necessary role in mediating nuclear entry of the PER/CRY complex in core clock regulation.
source: These data suggest a model in which KPNB1 plays a necessary role in mediating nuclear entry of the PER/CRY complex in core clock regulation (Figure 6).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all experimental data and illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Importin β emerged as a potential molecular target for cancer prevention.
source: Recently, importin β emerged as a potential molecular target for cancer prevention (van der Watt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Several novel small molecule regulators of KPNB1 have been identified.
source: So far, several novel small molecule regulators of KPNB1 have been identified, though further investigation is needed to improve their specificity and efficacy (Hintersteiner et al., 2010; Soderholm et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: This study provides a rationale for KPNB1 as molecular target for regulating clock physiology.
source: In this respect, our study provides a rationale for KPNB1 as molecular target for regulating clock physiology.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the potential applications of the study findings.
